pki-alma-csr:1.title: Step 1: Prepare the request settings
pki-alma-csr:1.where: AlmaLinux application VM · Terminal · your authorized account
pki-alma-csr:1.why: SAN is the list of website names the certificate should cover.
pki-alma-csr:1.needs: Complete the preceding chapter and keep your change notes beside you.
actions: In the AlmaLinux Terminal, type mkdir -p ~/pki-work and press Enter. Then type curl --fail --location https://cloudseam.tech/pki-lab/req.cnf --output ~/pki-work/req.cnf and press Enter. Stop if the download fails. To edit the file, type vi ~/pki-work/req.cnf and press Enter; press i to enter insert mode, edit only the approved CN and DNS.1 names, press Esc, then type :wq and press Enter to save and close.
Create ~/pki-work. Download the CSR settings file below into that folder as req.cnf.

Open it in your text editor. In this private example CN and DNS.1 are app.example.mil. For an organization request, use only its approved real name and required subject fields. Keep the CN and SAN consistent.
Confirm every needed DNS name with the application owner and PKI team. Adding a name to a CSR does not create DNS or authorize ownership.

pki-alma-validate:1.title: Step 1: Update only the intended site and test before reload
pki-alma-validate:1.where: AlmaLinux application VM · Terminal · your authorized account
pki-alma-validate:1.why: Keep the application configuration and old recovery pair intact.
pki-alma-validate:1.needs: Complete the preceding chapter and keep your change notes beside you.
actions: In the Terminal, type sudoedit followed by one space and the complete NGINX site-file path you recorded in the inventory step. For example, use sudoedit /etc/nginx/conf.d/app.conf only if that is the file your nginx -T output identified. The filename is your recorded value; the sudoedit command is fixed syntax.

Open the recorded site configuration with sudoedit. In its existing HTTPS server block, set ssl_certificate to /etc/pki/tls/certs/sonic-app-v1-fullchain.pem and ssl_certificate_key to /etc/pki/tls/private/sonic-app-v1.key.

For a previously HTTP-only prepared application, add its approved private HTTPS binding with listen 443 ssl and server_name app.example.mil while preserving the real application locations. Do not paste a static-site block over an application proxy.
Run nginx -t. Reload only if it passes. Check service status and logs. Do not disable SELinux, firewalld or validation to obtain a green result.

pki-alma-validate:2.where: Private test client · Terminal with OpenSSL and curl
pki-alma-validate:2.why: SNI selects the named site; hostname and trust checks verify its identity.

pki-iis-csr:1.title: Step 1: Prepare the SAN-aware request file
pki-iis-csr:1.why: The browser matches DNS names in Subject Alternative Name.
pki-iis-csr:1.needs: Complete the preceding chapter and keep your change notes beside you.
actions: Inside the application VM, open Start → Windows PowerShell → Run as administrator. Type New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path C:\SONIC-PKI -Force. Then type Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Uri https://cloudseam.tech/pki-lab/iis-request.inf -OutFile C:\SONIC-PKI\iis-request.inf. After the download succeeds, type notepad.exe C:\SONIC-PKI\iis-request.inf to inspect the settings.
Create C:\SONIC-PKI on the application VM. Download iis-request.inf below into that folder.
Open the INF in Notepad. Confirm Subject CN and the DNS SAN are tickets.lab.example.test for private practice, or your organization’s approved names. Confirm the key algorithm and PKI policy.

MachineKeySet = TRUE creates the machine-context key; Exportable = FALSE keeps this practice key non-exportable. HashAlgorithm = sha256 signs the request. These are not the validity dates of the returned certificate.
The IIS Manager Create Certificate Request wizard is another entry point, but do not assume its subject form adds your required SANs. This class uses certreq and then verifies the actual request.
